questions.title: Generics practice 1
questions.prompt: Which declaration creates a list that accepts Integer values?
choices: List<Integer> scores = new ArrayList<>();
List<int> scores = new ArrayList<>();
List scores<Integer> = new ArrayList<>();
Integer<List> scores = new ArrayList<>();
questions.explanation: The element type belongs inside angle brackets after List. Collections use the wrapper type Integer rather than the primitive type int.

questions.title: Generics practice 2
choices: A type chosen when Box is used
A required class named T
The number of items in the box
A private text value
questions.explanation: T is a placeholder for a reference type. Declaring Box<String> replaces T with String for that use of the class.

questions.title: Trace Generics
questions.prompt: What output does this code produce? Enter each line in order.
questions.explanation: This list accepts String values. Getting an item returns a String, so no cast is needed. The resulting output is 'CS101'.

questions.title: Generics practice 5
questions.prompt: Why does `List<String> names` catch a wrong-type mistake that the raw `List values` does not?
choices: The element type is checked at compile time, so adding the wrong type fails to compile
A raw list cannot hold objects at all
get(0) on a raw list always returns null
The generic list sorts its items automatically
questions.explanation: `List<String>` tells the compiler only strings belong, so `names.add(42)` would not compile and `get` returns a String with no cast. The raw `List` accepts anything and defers the problem to a cast that can blow up at run time. Generics add type checking, not sorting, and a raw list still stores objects.

questions.title: Wrapper types in generics
questions.prompt: Why does Java use `Integer` instead of `int` inside `List<Integer>`?
choices: Collections use wrapper types like `Integer` and `Double`, not primitives like `int`.
Use raw collection types and hope casts are correct.
Put primitive types directly inside generic angle brackets.
Store mixed unrelated types in one typed collection.
questions.explanation: Generics require reference types, so primitive values use wrapper types such as `Integer` and `Double`. Autoboxing makes most collection use feel natural, but the type written in angle brackets still has to be the wrapper.

questions.title: Typed collections
questions.prompt: Why should a Java collection usually declare its element type?
choices: Use a type parameter when only one concrete type is allowed.
Give every collection an element type.
Ignore compiler warnings about unchecked operations.
Cast every value instead of declaring the element type.
questions.explanation: A type such as `List<String>` lets the compiler reject the wrong kind of value before the program runs. Raw collections push those mistakes later, where they show up as casts or runtime errors.

questions.title: Primitive wrapper review
questions.prompt: A student wants a list of whole numbers. Which generic element type should they use?
choices: Use `Object` everywhere and give up type checking.
Forget that `Integer` is the wrapper for `int`.
Use wrapper types for primitive values.
Make the generic type name carry business meaning.
questions.explanation: `Integer` is the wrapper type for `int`, so it belongs inside generic angle brackets. The collection can still hold whole-number values, and Java handles much of the wrapping and unwrapping automatically.

questions.title: Avoid raw types
questions.prompt: What is the risk of using a raw `ArrayList` instead of `ArrayList<String>`?
choices: Return a raw list from a typed method.
Mix key and value type order in a map.
Assume generics change runtime values automatically.
Avoid raw collection types.
questions.explanation: A raw collection does not tell the compiler what element type is expected. That makes it easier to add the wrong kind of object and discover the problem only when code reads the value back.

questions.title: Diamond operator
questions.prompt: What does the diamond `<>` help with in a line such as `List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();`?
choices: Let the diamond `<>` copy the type from the declaration.
Use a generic class when a method parameter is enough.
Hide type errors until runtime by suppressing warnings.
Use one collection for values with different roles.
questions.explanation: The diamond lets Java infer the constructor's generic type from the declaration on the left. That keeps the type checked without repeating `String` twice in ordinary collection creation.

questions.title: Type parameter purpose
questions.prompt: When does a method or class need a generic type parameter such as `T`?
choices: Forget to type both sides of a relationship.
Use a type parameter when one design works for several types.
Treat `T` as a variable holding data.
Use generics to avoid naming the actual model.
questions.explanation: A type parameter is useful when one design works for several specific types while preserving type safety. It is not a data variable; it is a placeholder for a type the compiler tracks.
